title: A Simple Pre- and Post-Test Exercise (Unpack Outcomes Example)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a classroom-tested version of the Unpack Outcomes, Good or Bad strategy from The Will to Learn, applied around a world history test. Students write a warm-up before the test naming the specific actions they took to prepare and a target score, then after grading they return to that same writing to compare target versus actual results, plan changes for the next unit, and reflect on how the class is helping them grow beyond the test score itself. Stuart argues the specificity of the pre-test prompt matters because students default to vague answers like 'I studied' unless pushed toward naming concrete study behaviors, which builds the Effort belief, while naming a target score builds the Efficacy belief by letting students define success for themselves. He shares several handwritten student samples showing shifts from 'getting it done' to 'working to learn,' and frames the exercise as a low-prep, high-yield way to make a single test into a motivation-building experience rather than just a grade.
points: Pairing a pre-test warm-up (specific prep actions + target score) with a post-test reflection turns one test into a structured Effort-and-Efficacy-building exercise rather than a single data point.
Pushing students toward SPECIFIC study actions rather than vague answers like 'I studied' is itself a Woodenization move that makes effective effort visible and learnable.
Letting students set their own target score before the test builds the Efficacy belief because they are the ones defining what success looks like.
A 'Valued Within' question about growing stronger, more knowledgeable, and more capable pushes reflection past the test score toward the deeper purpose of the class.
Real student writing samples show the exercise working in practice, including a shift from viewing work as something to finish to something worth doing well.
quotes: By focusing on their inputs (the specific actions they took to prepare for the test), I'm setting the stage for them to be more thoughtful about their outputs (their test results).

This idea of SPECIFIC actions is very important because many of my ninth graders will default on questions like this to things like "I studied" or "I did not study." We want to be more specific than that.

Beyond test scores, how is this class giving you a chance to grow STRONGER, more KNOWLEDGEABLE, and more CAPABLE? This is a Valued Within exercise, as it gets them thinking about the WHY of the class in a deeper way than simple test scores.

He says, "What I did to prepare for the test was first I went over the flash cards, then I did the matching game, and then after I did the practice test." This is a great example of being specific about studying.
This student says that "By writing every day, we become more creative thinkers because we have the ability to put our thoughts down on a page freely.

She is realizing — through experience — that hard, smart work can get you a better outcome. That is an incredibly powerful realization, the impact of which will never be measurable on the kinds of standardized tests that we use to judge schools but that is nonetheless incredibly important at the scale of a human life.
